proof_skeleton_nl: Normalize the original summand by the elementary identity in Lemma L1, so the theorem sum becomes the normalized rational sum S(q) whose only summand denominators are (-q^d;q^d)_k. Clear these denominators by the common factor D(q) to form H(q)=D(q)S(q). The first substantive input, Lemma L3, shows that H(q) is a Laurent polynomial divisible by [n]_q, so H(q)=[n]_q J(q). Independently, Lemma L4 factors the claimed right-hand side as [n]_q G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2}. The bottleneck Lemma L6 then compares the quotient J(q) with D(q)G(q)q^{r(1-n)/2} at every primitive nth root of unity, including first derivative. Lemma L5 converts that first-order root-of-unity comparison into Φ_n(q)^2-divisibility of the quotient difference. Multiplying back by [n]_q gives divisibility of D(q)(S(q)-R(q)) by [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2. Finally, Lemma L2 shows that D(q) and the normalized denominators are coprime to the modulus, and Lemma L7 cancels D(q) in the localized congruence ring. Replacing S(q) by the original theorem sum using Lemma L1 yields the required congruence.

steps.derives: From the theorem hypotheses n > 1 and n ≡ 1 mod 2d, conclude that n is odd and gcd(d,n)=1.
steps.trivial_justification: Write n = 1 + 2dt for some integer t. Then n is odd. If a positive integer c divides both d and n, then c also divides n - 2dt = 1, so c = 1. Therefore gcd(d,n)=1.

steps.derives: Define T(q) = ∑_{k=0}^{n-1} [3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k^2 q^{k(d-dk-2r)/2} / (q^{2d};q^{2d})_k, define S(q) = ∑_{k=0}^{n-1} [3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k q^{k(d-dk-2r)/2} / (-q^d;q^d)_k, define R(q) = [rn]_q q^{r(1-n)/2}, define D(q) = ∏_{s=0}^{n-1} (-q^d;q^d)_s, define H(q) = D(q)S(q), define G(q) = ∑_{j=0}^{r-1} q^{jn}, and define M(q) = [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2.
steps.trivial_justification: This step only introduces abbreviations for the original sum, the normalized sum, the right-hand side, the clearing factor, the cleared sum, the geometric quotient, and the target modulus.

Lemma L1 rewrites the factor ((q^d;q^d)_k)^2/(q^{2d};q^{2d})_k in each summand of T(q) as (q^d;q^d)_k/(-q^d;q^d)_k. After this termwise replacement, the resulting sum is exactly the definition of S(q).

steps.derives: There exists a Laurent polynomial J(q) in Z[q^{±1}] such that H(q) = [n]_q J(q).
steps.trivial_justification: Lemma L3 states that H(q) belongs to Z[q^{±1}] and is divisible by [n]_q in that ring. By the definition of divisibility, a quotient J(q) exists with H(q) = [n]_q J(q).

steps.derives: R(q) = [n]_q G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2}, and therefore D(q)R(q) = [n]_q D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2}.
steps.trivial_justification: Lemma L4 gives [rn]_q = [n]_q G(q). Substituting this identity into the definition R(q) = [rn]_q q^{r(1-n)/2} yields the first formula. Multiplying by D(q) gives the second formula.

From A1, H(q)=D(q)S(q). Hence D(q)(S(q)-R(q)) = H(q) - D(q)R(q). By A3, H(q) = [n]_q J(q). By A4, D(q)R(q) = [n]_q D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2}. Substituting these two identities into H(q)-D(q)R(q) gives [n]_q J(q) - [n]_q D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2}, and factoring out [n]_q yields the displayed identity.

steps.derives: If B(q) = D(q) q^{r(1-n)/2} G(q), then for every primitive nth root of unity ζ one has J(ζ) = B(ζ) and J'(ζ) = B'(ζ).
steps.trivial_justification: Step A3 provides exactly the hypothesis H(q) = [n]_q J(q) required by Lemma L6, and the definitions of D(q), H(q), and G(q) in A1 match the objects in that lemma. Therefore Lemma L6 gives the stated equalities of values and derivatives at primitive nth roots.

steps.derives: Φ_n(q)^2 divides J(q) - D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2} in Z[q^{±1}].
steps.trivial_justification: Apply Lemma L5 with A(q)=J(q) and B(q)=D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2}. Step A6 supplies the hypotheses that A and B have equal values and equal first q-derivatives at every primitive nth root of unity.

steps.derives: M(q) divides [n]_q ( J(q) - D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2} ) in Z[q^{±1}].
steps.trivial_justification: By A1, M(q) = [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2. Step A7 says that Φ_n(q)^2 divides the parenthesized Laurent polynomial. Multiplying that divisibility by [n]_q gives the displayed divisibility by M(q).

steps.derives: M(q) divides D(q)(S(q)-R(q)); equivalently, D(q)S(q) ≡ D(q)R(q) mod M(q).
steps.trivial_justification: Step A5 identifies D(q)(S(q)-R(q)) exactly with [n]_q ( J(q) - D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2} ). Step A8 says that M(q) divides this latter Laurent polynomial. Replacing the right-hand side in A5 by the equal expression therefore shows M(q) divides D(q)(S(q)-R(q)). Since the divisor M(q) has constant term 1, this is precisely the localized congruence D(q)S(q) ≡ D(q)R(q) mod M(q).

steps.derives: The polynomial D(q), a common denominator for S(q), and the denominator of R(q) are all coprime to M(q).
steps.trivial_justification: By A3, H(q) is a Laurent polynomial, and by A1 we have S(q)=H(q)/D(q). Thus D(q) is a common denominator for S(q). Step A0 gives that n is odd and gcd(d,n)=1, so Lemma L2 applies and yields gcd(D(q),M(q))=1. Hence the chosen denominator of S(q) is coprime to M(q). For R(q)=[rn]_q q^{r(1-n)/2}, the exponent r(1-n)/2 is an integer because n is odd, so the denominator of R(q) is a power of q. Finally M(q)=[n]_q Φ_n(q)^2 has constant term 1, because [n]_q has constant term 1 and Φ_n(q) has constant term 1 for n>1; therefore q is coprime to M(q). So the denominator of R(q) is also coprime to M(q).

Step A9 gives D(q)S(q) ≡ D(q)R(q) mod M(q). Step A10 verifies the hypotheses needed to apply Lemma L7: D(q) is coprime to M(q), and the denominators of S(q) and R(q) are coprime to M(q). Therefore Lemma L7, applied with F(q)=S(q), G(q)=R(q), D(q)=D_{d,n}(q), and M(q)=[n]_q Φ_n(q)^2, implies S(q) ≡ R(q) mod M(q).

steps.derives: Let [m]_q = (1−q^m)/(1−q), let (a;q)_k = ∏_{j=0}^{k−1} (1−aq^j), let (a,b,c;q)_k = (a;q)_k (b;q)_k (c;q)_k, and let Φ_n(q) be the nth cyclotomic polynomial. Prove that for positive integers d and r with gcd(d,r)=1 and r ≤ d, and for every integer n > 1 with n ≡ 1 mod 2d, we have ∑_{k=0}^{n−1} [3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k^2 q^(k(d−dk−2r)/2) / (q^{2d};q^{2d})_k ≡ [rn]_q q^(r(1−n)/2) mod [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2.
steps.trivial_justification: Step A2 identifies the original theorem sum T(q) with the normalized sum S(q). Step A11 gives S(q) ≡ R(q) mod M(q). Substituting back the definitions of T(q), R(q), and M(q) yields exactly the root theorem statement.
